28 April
The Soi Nhụ culture appeared.
The Ngườm culture appeared.
The Sơn Vi culture appeared in modern Lâm Thao district.
Hoabinhian artifacts began to be produced in Northern Vietnam.
The Bắc Sơn culture appeared.
The Quỳnh Văn culture appeared.
The Cái Bèo culture appeared.
The first rice cultivation of which evidence survives in modern Vietnam took place.
The Đa Bút culture appeared in what is now Vĩnh Lộc district.
Wet rice was cultivated in the Red River Delta.

Kinh Dương Vương unified all vassal states in his territory into the single state of Xích Quỷ, which he ruled as Hùng king from the capital at Phong Châu. He also sponsored the development of martial arts in Xích Quỷ at the time.
Kinh Dương Vương was succeeded as Hùng king of Xích Quỷ, since renamed Văn Lang, by his son Lạc Long Quân.
The lunar calendar came into use in Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Cấn line came to power in Văn Lang.
The Hùng king ordered an increase in rice cultivation.
The last Hùng king of the Cấn line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Chấn line came to power in Văn Lang.
The earliest surviving artifacts indicating use of the Vietnamese calendar appeared.
The Phùng Nguyên culture appeared.
The last Hùng king of the Chấn line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Tốn line came to power in Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Ly line came to power in Văn Lang.
Burial rituals and tomb building came into practice.
The first Hùng king of the Khôn line came to power in Văn Lang.
The Đồng Đậu culture appeared.
A sophisticated agricultural society developed on the Vietnamese coast.
The last Hùng king of the Khôn line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Đoài line came to power in Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Giáp line came to power in Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Ất line came to power in Văn Lang.
The Lạc Việt discovered bronze casting.
Irrigation was first used in rice cultivation in the plains of the Mã and Red Rivers.
The last Hùng king of the Ất line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Bính line came to power in Văn Lang.
The Gò Mun culture appeared.
The last Hùng king of the Bính line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Đinh line came to power in Văn Lang.
The Đông Sơn culture appeared in the valley of the Red River.
Copper casting began to be used in Văn Lang in the manufacture of brass tools, weapons, and ornaments.
The population of Văn Lang reached one million.
The Lạc Việt developed observational astronomy.
The last Hùng king of the Đinh line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Mậu line came to power in Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Kỷ line came to power in Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Canh line came to power in Văn Lang.
Refugees from the increasingly fragile Zhou dynasty began to arrive in the Red River Delta.
The last Hùng king of the Canh line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Tân line came to power in Văn Lang.
The metallurgical style unique to the Đông Sơn drums was invented.
An elaborate system of canals and dikes was invented which made possible the tidal irrigation of rice fields.
The last Hùng king of the Tân line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
The first Hùng king of the Nhâm line came to power in Văn Lang.
The earliest artifacts suggesting the celebration of Tết appeared.
King Goujian of Yue sent messengers to Văn Lang demanding submission.
The last Hùng king of the Nhâm line ended his rule of Văn Lang.
Hùng Duệ Vương became Hùng king of Văn Lang.
A mass migration of refugees to the Red River Delta took place due to the ongoing collapse of the Zhou dynasty.
Buddhist missionaries from Maurya Empire arrived in Văn Lang.
The Âu Việt settled across the northern border of Văn Lang and opened trade relations with the Lạc Việt.
Thục Phán, ruler of the Âu Việt, invaded and conquered Văn Lang. He renamed the country Âu Lạc and took the regnal name An Dương Vương, ruling as king from Cổ Loa Citadel.
The Hùng Temple was built.
The Battle of Tiên Du took place.
The Qin general Zhao Tuo captured Cổ Loa Citadel. An Dương Vương fled and later committed suicide.
Zhao Tuo divided the territory under his control into the commanderies of Jiaozhi and Jiuzhen.Chinese annals mark this as the start of Vietnamese history.
The warlord Xiang Yu led an army into the Qin capital Xianyang, burned the Epang Palace and killed the Qin emperor Ziying and the royal family.
Zhao Tuo declared himself king of Nanyue, with his capital in modern Panyu, Guangzhou.
Nanyue conquered Guilin.
Two delegates were assigned to oversee the affairs of Jiaozhi and Jiuzhen.
The Han official Lu Jia gave Zhao Tuo a seal recognizing him as king of Nanyue in exchange for his nominal submission to the Han emperor.
Empress Lü, the Han empress dowager and regent for her grandson Emperor Houshao of Han, ordered a trade blockade of Nanyue.
Zhao Tuo sacked the Han capital Chang'an.
The nearby polities of Minyue, Yelang and Tongshi declared their allegiance to Nanyue.
A punitive Han invasion of Nanyue stalled after much of the invading army fell to illness.
Lü Zhi died. Nanyue conquered some Han territory near the border.

In exchange for the restoration of his family in modern Zhengding County and the withdrawal of Han forces from the Nanyue border, Zhao Tuo renounced the title emperor and pledged submission to the Han dynasty.
Luy Lâu was founded.
Zhao Tuo died. He was succeeded as king of Nanyue by his grandson Zhao Mo.
A border war took place between Nanyue and Minyue.
Zhao Mo died. He was succeeded as king of Nanyue by his eldest son Zhao Yingqi.
Confucian ideas were introduced to Nanyue.
Zhao Yingqi died. He was succeeded by his son Zhao Xing.

Lü Jia, the prime minister of Nanyue and a Lạc Việt chief, killed Zhao Xing and his Han Chinese mother Juishi after the latter agreed to full submission to the Han dynasty in order to preserve her authority in Nanyue. He declared Zhao Xing's elder brother Zhao Jiande king.

Han conquest of Nanyue: Han forces invaded Nanyue. Zhao Jiande was captured in flight and executed. The zhou of Jiaozhou was organized on the territory of the defunct Nanyue and divided into the commanderies of Nanhai, Cangwu, Yulin, Jiaozhi, Hepu, Zhuya, Taner, and Jiuzhen. Shi Dai was appointed its governor.
Tây Vu Vương launched a revolt against Han forces.
Tây Vu Vương was assassinated by his assistant Hoàng Đồng.
Shi Dai's rule of Jiaozhou ended.
The commandery of Rinan in Jiaozhou was organized south of the Hoành Sơn Range.
Tích Quang became governor of Jiaozhou.
A census in Jiaozhou counted some hundred thousand households and nearly one million people.
Tích Quang's rule of Jiaozhou ended.
Su Ding became governor of Jiaozhou.
Thi Sách was assassinated.
Trung sisters' rebellion: The Trưng Sisters launched a rebellion against Han authority in the Red River Delta.
Trung sisters' rebellion: the Trưng Sisters committed suicide by drowning themselves before The Han general Ma Yuan could capture them.
Sun Quan declared himself emperor, founding the state of Eastern Wu, separating from the Han dynasty.
Lady Triệu uprising.
Following his rebellion and expulsion of Liang forces from Jiaozhou, Lý Nam Đế was proclaimed emperor of Vạn Xuân.

The Liang general Emperor Wu of Chen launched a surprise attack on the Vạn Xuân capital Long Biên, forcing Lý Nam Đế and the imperial administration to flee to the Gia Ninh Citadel in modern Việt Trì.
Lý Nam Đế was forced to retreat to Khuất Lão Cave, where he reorganized his army under the command of Triệu Việt Vương.
Vạn Xuân forces defended Dạ Trạch in modern Khoái Châu District from Liang forces.
Lý Nam Đế ceded rule of Vạn Xuân to Triệu Việt Vương and his older brother Lý Thiên Bảo.
Lý Nam Đế was assassinated in modern Laos.
Triệu Việt Vương expelled Liang forces from Vạn Xuân and reestablished the capital at Long Biên.
Lý Thiên Bảo died without heirs.
Hậu Lý Nam Đế, Lý Nam Đế's cousin and claimant to the throne of Vạn Xuân, signed a truce with Triệu Việt Vương establishing a boundary between their two territories.
Hậu Lý Nam Đế surprised and conquered Triệu Việt Vương and moved his capital to Phong Châu.
Sui–Former Lý War: Sui conquered Vạn Xuân following a brief rebellion by Hậu Lý Nam Đế.
Mai Thúc Loan uprising.
Phùng Hưng uprising.

Battle of Bạch Đằng: Ngô Quyền defeated the Southern Han kingdom at the Battle of Bạch Đằng north of modern Haiphong and ended 1,000 years of Chinese domination dating back to 111 BC under the Han dynasty, founding the Ngô dynasty.
Anarchy of the 12 Warlords

Emperor Đinh Bộ Lĩnh of Đại Cồ Việt was assassinated along with his crown prince Đinh Liễn by a minor palace official. His surviving son, the young Đinh Phế Đế, succeeded him under the regency of the commander-in-chief Lê Hoàn.
Lê Hoàn declared himself viceroy of Đại Cồ Việt with the support of the empress dowager Dương Vân Nga.
The nobles Nguyễn Bặc and Đinh Điền attacked the Đại Cồ Việt capital Hoa Lư in response to Lê Hoàn's apparent usurpation.
Nguyễn Bặc and Đinh Điền were executed.
Lê Hoàn declared himself emperor at Hoa Lư.
Battle of Bạch Đằng (981): Đại Cồ Việt forces defeated a Song invasion near Lạng Sơn, forcing the Song fleet on the Bạch Đằng River to withdraw.
Nam quốc sơn hà, a poem celebrating the sovereignty of Đại Cồ Việt over its territory, was written.
Đại Cồ Việt forces sacked the Champa capital Indrapura.
Lê Hoàn died.
The imperial court acclaimed Lý Thái Tổ emperor of Đại Cồ Việt.
Lý Thái Tổ issued the chiếu dời đô, an edict ordering the transfer of the capital from Hoa Lư to Đại La.
Lý Thái Tổ's son Lý Thái Tông became emperor of Đại Cồ Việt.
The Nùng warlord Nùng Tồn Phúc launched a failed rebellion against Lý Thái Tông.
Lý Thái Tông died. He was succeeded by his son Lý Thánh Tông.
The Temple of Literature, Hanoi, a Confucian temple, was constructed.
Lý Thánh Tông died. He was succeeded as emperor by his young son Lý Nhân Tông, with the latter's mother Ỷ Lan and the chancellor Lý Đạo Thành acting as regents.
Minor officials were chosen by examination for the first time.
Lý–Song War: Đại Cồ Việt invaded Song in response to a trade blockade.
Lý Nhân Tông died.
The young Lý Cao Tông became emperor under the regency of Tô Hiến Thành.
The general Quách Bốc entered the capital, dethroned Lý Cao Tông and installed his young son Lý Thẩm as emperor.
Trần Thái Tông was crowned emperor of Đại Việt.
Mongol invasions of Vietnam: The Mongol Empire invaded Đại Việt and conquered the capital at modern Hanoi. Trần Thái Tông fled to an island.
Trần Thánh Tông ceded the throne to his son Trần Nhân Tông.
The Bình Than Conference took place.
The Diên Hồng Conference took place.
Mongol invasions of Vietnam: The Đại Việt commander-in-chief Trần Hưng Đạo drew out and harassed a Yuan invasion force, forcing their retreat.
Mongol invasions of Vietnam: The Mongol navy was destroyed, forcing the army, left without provisions, to begin its retreat from Đại Việt.
Trần Nhân Tông ceded the throne to his son Trần Anh Tông.
Trần Anh Tông's sister Huyền Trân married the Champa king Chế Mân in Huế.
The young Trần Dụ Tông was crowned emperor of Đại Việt under the regency of his father, the retired emperor Trần Minh Tông.
Champa launched several border attacks against Đại Việt.
Hồ Quý Ly overthrew the Đại Việt emperor, enthroned himself, renamed the country Đại Ngu and moved the capital to the citadel of the Hồ dynasty.
The Cham-Vietnamese War (1400–1407) began.
Hồ Quý Ly ceded the throne to his son Hồ Hán Thương.
Ming–Hồ War: Ming forces captured the Đại Ngu capitals.
Lê Lợi was declared emperor of an independent Đại Việt.
The Bình Ngô đại cáo was published, affirming that Đại Việt was independent from and equal to China.
Lê Thánh Tông was crowned emperor of Đại Việt.
The Đại Việt sử ký toàn thư, an official history of Đại Việt, was completed.
The Hồng Đức legal code was promulgated.
Lê Thánh Tông died.
Lê Oanh assassinated his cousin, the tyrant Lê Uy Mục, and replaced him as emperor Lê Tương Dực.
The Trần Tuân Uprising took place.
Trần Cao rebellion: Trần Cao, a mandarin of Đại Việt who identified himself as an incarnation of Śakra, launched a revolt against the government.
Portuguese seafarers arrived.
Lê Tương Dực was murdered in the capital by a group of palace guards.
Mạc Đăng Dung forced Emperor Lê Cung Hoàng to abdicate, establishing the Mạc dynasty.
Lê–Mạc War.
The Revival Lê dynasty defeated the Mạc dynasty and regained control of the country.
Trịnh–Nguyễn War.
The forces of the Tây Sơn dynasty took Gia Định in modern Saigon and massacred the Nguyễn lords, the de facto rulers of southern Đại Việt, sparing only the young Nguyễn Thế Tổ.
Nguyễn Văn Nhạc proclaimed himself emperor of Đại Việt with his capital at Quy Nhơn.
Nguyễn Thế Tổ fled the country.

Battle of Rạch Gầm-Xoài Mút: Đại Việt forces under a banner of truce surprised and defeat a Siamese force, then invade with the intention of installing Nguyễn Thế Tổ on the throne, on the Mekong River in modern Tiền Giang Province.
The Phú Xuân Campaign (1786) took place.
The Thăng Long Campaign took place.
The Nguyễn Nhạc-Nguyễn Huệ split occurred.

The French priest Pierre Pigneau de Behaine signed the Treaty of Versailles on behalf of Nguyễn Thế Tổ. The French government agreed to support the latter in taking the throne of Đại Việt in exchange for Côn Sơn Island and exclusive trading rights.
Battle of Ngọc Hồi-Đống Đa: Qing forces invaded Đại Việt in support of the deposed emperor Lê Chiêu Thống.
Nguyễn Văn Nhạc's younger brother Nguyễn Văn Huệ proclaimed himself emperor of Đại Việt. Nguyễn Văn Nhạc relinquished the title, taking that of king instead.
Nguyễn Thế Tổ conquered Gia Định in modern Saigon.
The Battle of Bình Thuận took place.
Nguyễn Văn Huệ died, probably from a stroke. He was succeeded by his young son Nguyễn Quang Toản.
The Siege of Quy Nhơn took place.
Battle of Thị Nại.
Battle of Trấn Ninh
The Nguyễn defeat last of Tây Sơn forces.
Capital moved to Huế.
Emperor Cảnh Thịnh died, Emperor Gia Long became ruler of Vietnam.
Tang thương ngẫu lục (Random Record of Great Changes) is finalized.
Nguyễn Du completes The Tale of Kieu.
Hoàng Việt law enforced.
Emperor Gia Long (1802–1820) ended his rule of Vietnam.
Emperor Minh Mạng (1820–1841) became ruler of Vietnam.
Phan Bá Vành Uprising.
Nông Văn Vân Uprising.
Lê Văn Khôi Revolt.
Emperor Minh Mạng (1820–1841) ended his rule of Vietnam.
Emperor Thiệu Trị (1841–1847) became ruler of Vietnam.
USS Constitution lands in Da Nang as a company of US Marines moves overland to Huế and rescues a French Bishop who had been captured by the Vietnamese.
French bombardment of Da Nang in response to persecution of Catholic missionaries.
Emperor Thiệu Trị (1841–1847) ended his rule of Vietnam.
Emperor Tự Đức (1847–1883) became ruler of Vietnam.
Cao Bá Quát Uprising.
Cochinchina Campaign.
Thủ Khoa Huân Uprising.
Sinking of L'Esperance
Trương Định Uprising.
Treaty of Saigon.
The French establishes the colony of Cochinchina.
Discovery of Quang Yen coalfield
Emperor Tự Đức (1847–1883) ended his rule of Vietnam.
Ruler: Emperor Hàm Nghi (1884–1885)
Battle of the Huế Imperial City. Hàm Nghi leads resistance.
Emperor Đồng Khánh (1885–1889) became ruler of Vietnam.
Cần Vương Movement.
Hàm Nghi captured and exiled to Algeria.
Emperor Đồng Khánh (1885–1889) ended his rule of Vietnam.
Films about Vietnamese history
Ruler: Emperor Thành Thái (1889–1907)
Đông Du Movement.
The Duy Tân movement, initiated by Phan Châu Trinh, was launched.
Ruler: Emperor Khải Định (1916–1925)
Thái Nguyên uprising.
Emperor Bảo Đại (r. 1926–1945) became ruler of Vietnam.
Nghệ Tĩnh Revolt.
Communist Party of Vietnam (CPV) is the founding and ruling communist party of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam.
Tenth National Party Congress.
Trần Đức Lương (1997–2006) resigns as President of Vietnam, replaced by Nguyễn Minh Triết.
Admittance to World Trade Organization.
Eleventh National Party Congress.
President Nguyễn Minh Triết (2006–2011) ends his term, replaced by Trương Tấn Sang.
Amendment of Constitution. Democratic recommendations are ignored by the National Assembly. The new constitution comes into effect on the first day of next year.

Hai Yang Shi You 981 standoff: Tensions arises from the Chinese state-owned China National Offshore Oil Corporation moving its Hai Yang Shi You 981 oil platform to waters near the disputed Paracel Islands, resulting in large anti-China protests across Vietnam.
Vietnam's new marriage law goes into effect. Same-sex marriages are no longer prohibited, but are not recognized as being legally valid.
Twelfth National Party Congress.
President Trương Tấn Sang (2011–2016) ends his term, replaced by Trần Đại Quang.
2016 Vietnam marine life disaster.
First year of the COVID-19 pandemic in Vietnam.
Thirteenth National Party Congress. Unprecedented third term of the CPV General Secretary Nguyễn Phú Trọng starts.
The COVID-19 situations worsen significantly, particularly in Ho Chi Minh City.
Việt Á scandal, 'Rescue flights' scandal, and other corporate scandals are exposed.
Nguyễn Xuân Phúc resigns as President of Vietnam, replaced by Võ Văn Thưởng.
Trial of Trương Mỹ Lan and Van Thinh Phat Holdings Group.
Võ Văn Thưởng resigns as President of Vietnam, replaced by Tô Lâm.
CPV General Secretary Nguyễn Phú Trọng dies in his third term. Tô Lâm succeeds.
Tô Lâm resigns as President of Vietnam, replaced by Lương Cường.
Following the merger of administrative units, Vietnam has 34 provincial-level units, comprising 28 provinces and 6 centrally governed cities.
Fourteenth National Party Congress.
The oldest stone tools found in Thailand date to circa between 600,000 and 800,000 years ago, at Ban Mae Tha in Lampang province.

The Homo Erectus fossil called Lampang man is dated 500,000 BCE. It was discovered in Hat Pudai Village, Na Seng in Ko Kha district, Lampang, in 1999. Research shows that modern Thais and other Homo Sapiens in Southeast Asia are not related to Lampang man.
There are traces of human settlements in Thailand for 100,000 years.

The Youngest Toba eruption occurred circa 74,000 years ago. The Toba Supervolcano in North Sumatra produced 439–631 million tons of sulfuric acid. The air-fall of this eruption blanketed Thailand and Mainland Southeast Asia with a layer of 5–10 cm ash.

The Last Glacial Maximum was the coldest period of the Last Glacial Period between 26,000 and 20,000 years ago. The 3–4 km thick ice sheets in the Northern hemisphere lowered the sea level by about 120 meters. The climate was -6 Celsius colder than present in Thailand (between 12 and 32 °C). There were no ice sheets. There was no seawater in the Gulf of Thailand (max depth 85 m).
A skeleton of a woman dating to about 25,000 years ago was unearthed at Moh Khieo Cave in Muang district, Krabi province.
The Pleistocene (Last Glacial Period (LGP)) ends around 11,700 years ago (before present).

Neolithic culture appears in many parts of Thailand: Spirit Cave (Mae Hong Son) Lang Kamnan Cave and Wang Bhodi (Kanchanaburi), Khok Phanom Di (Chonburi), Khao Rakian (Songkhla), and in Ubon Ratchathani about 9000 BCE.

The Ban Chiang culture flourishes. This Bronze Age pre-Thai civilization was discovered in an archeological site situated in the Khorat plateau of Udon Thani province in the northeast of Thailand. The oldest bronze artefacts and grave date to 2100 BCE.
Recent archaeological excavations suggests that domesticated rice was introduced to Central Thailand by immigrating rice farming societies about 2050 BCE.
Dugout wooden coffins with human skeletons for the burial ritual of cave people were found at Ong Ba Cave in Kanchanaburi province dated 2,500-4,000 years ago.
Artifacts of the earliest agricultural communities in present-day Thailand circa 4,000 years ago.

Iron tools and weapons were found in the archeological sites: Non Nok Tha (1420 to 50 BCE), Lopburi Artillery centre (1225 to 700 BCE), Ong Ba Cave (310 to 150 BCE), Ban Don Ta Phet (24 BCE to 276 CE) (see Prehistoric Thailand).
The semi-legendary Singhanavati Kingdom is founded along the Kok River in the Chiang Rai basin (Northern Thailand). It existed from circa 691 BCE to 638 CE.
Chinese T’ai migration recorded. Beginning of the migration of Tai people south towards Mainland Southeast Asia. These migrants speak Tai languages.
Southern Thailand has evidence of rice agriculture from 2500 - 2200 B.P (550 BCE - 250 BCE).
Indian settlements bring the Hindu religion to the region in Southeast Asia.

Buddhism reaches places in the region such as Nakhon Pathom from India as propagated by the Mauryan Emperor Ashoka. He sent monks during his reign to popularize Theravada Buddhism (268-232 BC). This is evident by excavated ruins in the city Nakhon Pathom in Thailand.

An earthquake causes Chiang Saen Lake to submerge the capital city of Singhanavati in Yonok Nahaphan (Chiang Saen District, Chiang Rai). The capital is moved to Vieng Prueksa [th] (Fang District). There is a submerged town "Wiang Nong Lom" (เวียงหนองหล่ม, "drowned town") in a swamp south of the lake.
The Singhanavati Kingdom evolves into the Northern Thai Ngoenyang Kingdom during the fourteen chiefdoms era (545–638).

The first king of the Siamese dynasty is called Phraborom Suriyathep Northai Suwannabophit (Thai: พระบรมสุริยเทพนรไทยสุวรรณบพิตร) according to the record of Simon de la Loubère. His court is in Chaiburi Mahanakhon (Thai: ไชยบุรีมหานคร). Loubère did not know the exact location. His reign begins in 757 CE (1300 Buddhist Era).
In the 9th century, the first Muslim merchants settle in the Malay Peninsula including the area that was the southern part of Siam.

The Mons from Burma settle in Central Thailand. A monarchy with a unified Thai kingdom called Ayutthaya is established by King Uthong (Ramathibodi I). A series of kings follow who rule what becomes known as Siam.
The Siamese city-state Suphannabhum is founded circa 1150.
In the 13th century many Tais flee present-day Myanmar and China to escape the Mongol armies of Kublai Khan.
Sukhothai is taken by the Thais from the Khmers in 1220 and made their capital.
Khmer power wanes in the region. The Khmer are overthrown by Tai chieftains in Sukhothai. The Khmer rule is abolished and replaced by the Sukhothai Kingdom which is founded by Si Inthrathit in 1238.
The Thai-speaking Sukhothai kingdom expands its rule further south to dominate much of modern-day Thailand, before being eclipsed by a rival Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya.

The Mongol Armies led by Kublai Khan conquer the Kingdom of Nanzhao in southern China in 1253. This causes a mass migration including Tai warriors who consolidate the independent Tai states. Ayutthaya is reinforced by the Tai migrants which ensures Tai supremacy over the Khmer in the Central Plain.
The rule of King Ramkhamhaeng is established in Sukhothai. Sukhothai is a small local power until its third rule in the year 1279. Sukhothai's power expands into the Malay Peninsula.

The reign of King Ramkhamhaeng is marked by major advancements and the inception of a unified Thai identity. This begins with the creation and utilization of the Thai script in 1283 and significant flourishing of the arts. Ram Khamhaeng made major contributions to Thai governance, culture and religion. The people in the Central Plain call themselves "Thai" to distinguish themselves as freed Tai people from others under foreign rule.
Siamese begin to occupy the northern Malay Peninsula. Negara Sri Dharmaraja and Patani, become Siamese vassals.
In 1281, the Thai Chiang Rai kingdom is founded and takes over power in northern Thailand.

King Ramkhamhaeng of Sukhothai pursues good relations with Kublai Khan and negotiates a treaty of amity with the Yuan dynasty in 1282.Ramkhamhaeng makes a personal visit to China to see Kublai Khan shortly before his death in 1294. The Mongols threaten to destroy Burma and Vietnam, but Sukhothai could prosper at their expense. The Mongols have no concern over Sukhothai and the later Lan Na Kingdom to the north is a buffer state.
The Thai ruler Mangrai from Mueang Ngoenyang unites several principalities and conquers the Mon Kingdom Haripunjaya in 1292. This is achieved with Tai war parties of the Northern Thai people.
The Lan Na kingdom is founded at Chiang Mai in 1292. The thriving Lan Na covers a large portion of northern Thailand and Laos which is controlled by King Mangrai.
A border dispute between the Lan Na kingdom and the Mongols causes a war in 1296. In 1301, the Mongols carry out an expedition which ends in a Mongol disaster.
The period ranging from 1298 to 1357 is marked as the slow decline and fall of the Sukhothai kingdom when the Lo Thai are rising to power in the city of Sukhothai.
The city of Ayutthaya is founded by Uthong (Ramathibodi I).
The sakdina system of social hierarchy is established at the beginning of Ayutthaya.
A Thai monarchy is established under the rule of King Ramathibodi which unifies the Ayutthaya kingdom. A series of kings follow, ruling what was then known as Siam.

The Ayutthaya kingdom rivals the Sukhothai kingdom and gradually brings Thailand under its control. Ayutthaya becomes a major power in Southeast Asia. Ayutthaya reached its greatest extent around 1600 by ruling over parts of modern-day Cambodia, Laos and Burma (Myanmar).
Prince Ramesuan of Ayutthaya conquers Chiang Mai in the north and Angkor the former capital of the Khmer Empire.
The Little Ice Age causes modest cooling in the Northern Hemisphere. The climate impact is negligible in Thailand and Southeast Asia.
A Khmer rebellion against the Suphannaphum-Mon dynasty of Ayutthaya results in a 7-month siege and the Fall of Angkor. This marks the end of the Angkorian period.

The fall of the Sukhothai kingdom. Sukhothai is virtually deserted. Power shifts to the Ayutthaya Kingdom. the Ayutthaya Kingdom is established on the ruins of the Sukhothai Empire, and it is the start of their rule.
Suphannabhum was completely annexed by Ayutthaya in 1438.
King Borommarachathirat II dies in 1448. Prince Ramesuan is crowned King Borommatrailokkanat of Ayutthaya, making a personal union between Sukhothai and Ayutthaya.
The Portuguese explorer Duarte Fernandes is the first European to arrive in the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1511. The Portuguese are theorized to have named the kingdom Siam.
The Portuguese send an envoy to the Thai Court and sign a treaty.

The Burmese–Siamese War (1547–1549) (aka the Shwehti war) was the first war fought between the Toungoo dynasty of Burma and the Ayutthaya Kingdom of Siam. Notable for the introduction of early modern warfare to the region and the Siamese Queen Suriyothai died in battle on her elephant. The Burmese–Siamese wars continued until the mid 19th century.
The Burmese and siamese agree to a truce which ended the Shwehti war in February 1549.
First-ever major warfare with the Mon Kingdom of Bago (Burma). The conflicts continue till 1569.

Burmese–Siamese War (1563–1564), (aka the War over the White Elephants), the 2nd Siege of Ayutthaya. After an extensive siege of the city of Ayutthaya, the Ayutthaya Kingdom becomes a vassal of the Toungoo dynasty for the first time. This vassal status lasts until 1568.
The first 2 Christian missionaries travel to Siam and arrive in Ayutthaya in 1567. These are the Dominicans Friar Jeronimo da Cruz and Sebastiao da Canto.
The Ayutthayans revolt against the Burmese rulers and briefly regain independence.

Burmese–Siamese War (1568–1569), (aka the War of the first fall) the 3rd Siege of Ayutthaya. Ayutthaya unsuccessfully attacked the Burmese vassal state Phitsanulok in 1568. The Burmese responded by intervening which resulted in the defeat of Ayutthaya on 2 August 1569. Ayutthaya became a Burmese vassal state again.
The Burmese capture and destroy Ayutthaya.

Burmese–Siamese War (1584–1593) (aka the Nandric War), the Fourth Siege of Ayutthaya. The Ayutthaya Kingdom declares independence in 1584, Burma invades Ayutthaya five times but is driven back each time (Siamese victory).

Naresuan becomes the 18th king of Ayutthaya in 1590. He abolishes a period of Burmese suzerainty. Ayuttaya expands rapidly to the detriment of the Burmese and Khmer realms. He also conquers Cambodia and parts of southern Burma.

Burmese–Siamese War (1593–1600) (aka the Naresuan War), The first Siamese invasion of Burma. Siam conquers the Tenasserim coastal region to Martaban. Lan Na (Chiang Mai) becomes a vassal of Siam, c. 1602.
Burmese–Siamese War (1609–1622), Wars of Nyaungyan restoration. Burma regains Martaban and Tavoy (1613), and Lan Na (1614).
Reign of King Prasat Thong. Trading concessions expand and regular trade with China and Europe is established.
The reign of King Narai starts in 1656. The influence of the British Empire expands. The reputation of Ayutthaya as a magnificent city and a remarkable royal court spreads in Europe.

Burmese–Siamese War (1662–1664), (aka Second Siamese Invasion of Burma). Siam briefly captures the upper Tenasserim coast to Martaban in 1662 before driven back. In 1663, Siam again invades upper Tenasserim coast and Lan Na, capturing Chiang Mai. Siamese forces evacuate Chiang Mai in 1664.
The first Siamese embassy to France composed of two Siamese ambassadors and Father Bénigne Vachet who left Siam for France on 5 January 1684.
The second Siamese embassy to France (1686) from Siam (Ayutthaya Kingdom). King Narai sent the embassy led by ambassador Kosa Pan.

The travel record Du royaume de Siam by French diplomat Simon de la Loubère is published. This is one of the few remaining records of the history and society of the Ayutthaya Kingdom in 1687. Most Thai chronicles were lost during the Burmese sacking of Ayutthaya in 1767.
Reign of King Borommakot. It is a period of peace, and of flourishing arts and literature.

Burmese–Siamese War (1759–1760) (aka the Alaungpaya's War) the Fifth Siege of Ayutthaya. Burma conquers the Tenasserim coastal region down to the Tavoy–Mergui frontier. Burma besieges the Ayutthaya, but returns home when their King is injured and becomes ill.

Burmese–Siamese War (1765–1767) (aka the War of the second fall of Ayutthaya), Burma invades Siam and besieges Ayutthaya. The invading Burmese forces sack the capital Ayutthaya city prior to being expunged by General Taksin. The Ayuthaya Kingdom collapses. Precious Thai historical records about the history of Siam were burned by the Burmese. The Burmese invasion force returned to Burma to defend their homeland against an imposing Chinese invasion of Ava.

Taksin's reunification of Siam (1767–1771). The fall of Ayuthaya left Siam divided into 5 separate states—Phimai, Phitsanulok, Sawangburi, Nakhon Si Thammarat, and Thonburi. The state of Thonburi, led by Taksin, prevailed, subjugating its rivals to successfully reunify Siam under the Thonburi Kingdom (1767–1782) by 1770/71. The capital is moved from Ayutthaya to Thonburi, near Bangkok. Phaya Taksin is crowned as King Taksin in 1767.
Thai control is re-established with the short-lived Thonburi Kingdom observed by King Taksin in 1768.

Siamese conquest of Lan Na (1774–1775). The Lan Na kingdom which was under Burmese rule for 2 centuries, is conquered by the Siamese armies of King Taksin of Thonburi. The Siamese take Burmese-held Chiang Mai in January 1775.

Bangkaeo Campaign (aka the Battle of Bangkaeo). The Burmese commander Maha Thiha Thura sent an expeditionary force to invade Western Siam through the Three Pagodas Pass. The Burmese force in Bangkaeo was encircled and defeated via starvation by the armies of Taksin.

Burmese–Siamese War (1775–1776) (aka the Athi Wungyi's War). Lan Na declares independence in 1775 with support of King Taksin. Burma invades Lan Na and Siam. After the death of King Hsinbyushin, the Burmese withdraw from Siam. The Siamese claim Lan Na which ends over 2 centuries of Burmese rule in 1776.
The city Chiang Mai is captured and the Burmese are expelled. The Emerald Buddha is brought from Vientiane in Laos, to Thonburi in Bangkok.
King Taksin is toppled by a coup launched by rebels and General Chao Phraya Chakri, who founds a new dynasty centered on Bangkok.

General Chao Phaya Chakri establishes the Chakri dynasty and assumes the name of Phra Phutthayotfa. He ascends the throne as King Rama I. The country is internationally known as Siam. The capital is moved across the river where Bangkok is founded.
Wat Phra Kaew, the temple of the Emerald Buddha is completed.

Burmese–Siamese War (1785–1786) (aka the Nine Armies' Wars). The first war between the Konbaung dynasty of Burma and the Siamese Rattanakosin Kingdom of the Chakri dynasty. The Burmese invaded with 9 armies consisting of 144,000 soldiers via 5 directions and were soundly defeated.

Tha Din Daeng campaign (aka the Tha Din Daeng War). A short conflict, occurring in 1786 in Tha Din Daeng, now Kanchanaburi province in western Thailand. The Rattanakosin forces of Phraphutthayotfa Chulalok and Maha Sura Singhanat destroy the Burmese belligerents of King Bodawpaya of the Konbaung Dynasty.
Tavoy campaign (1788). The Kingdom of Siam fails to reclaim the town of Tavoy and the Tenasserim Coast from the Burmese Konbaung dynasty.
Burmese–Siamese War (1792–1794) (aka the Siamese Invasion of Tavoy). Conflict where Siam fails to regain the lower Tenasserim Coast (Tavoy and Mergui).
Burmese–Siamese War (1797–1798). Burma invades Lan Na and besieges Chiang Mai. The city was taken, but King Kawila asks for reinforcement from Rama I, which helped them recapture the city.

Burmese–Siamese War (1802–1805). The Burmese forces of King Bodawpaya invade Chiang Mai in 1802. The Burmese are repelled by Prince Kawila with Siamese support. The Siamese under King Rama I retaliate and conquer the Burmese city Chiang Saen and the district in 1805.
The Kingdom of Chiang Mai is founded with the installation of Kawila in December 1802. This was a vassal state of the Rattanakosin Kingdom.

Burmese–Siamese War (1809–1812) (aka the Burmese Invasion of Thalang). The Burmese unsuccessfully attempt to capture Junk Ceylon. They are repelled by the Siamese in 1810 and 1812. The Kedah Sultanate helps Siam during the Burmese invasion of Tanjung Salang.
Siamese invasion of Kedah. The Rattanakosin Kingdom invades the Kedah Sultanate in November 1821. It results in a Siamese victory and direct Siamese rule on Kedah.
First trade treaty with Britain is signed. It was negotiated by John Crawfurd.

First Anglo-Burmese War. Conflict mostly between Burma and the United Kingdom. Siam is a nominal British ally. The Royal Siamese Army supports with 20,000 troops. Siam secures the Burney Treaty in 1826.
Burney Treaty is signed between Siam and the United Kingdom which partitions the northern Malay states between British Malaya and the Rattanakosin Kingdom.
First American envoy to the Thai Court. The United States and Siam (now Thailand) concluded a commercial treaty in Bangkok.
Siamese–Vietnamese War between King Rama III and Emperor Minh Mạng. Vietnam annexes eastern Cambodia (Tây Thành Province) in 1834.
Reign of King Mongkut (Rama IV). Mongkut accedes the throne in 1851. He embraces Western innovations and initiates the modernization of Thailand. King Mongkut accedes in 1851.
Bowring treaty signed between the United Kingdom and Siam.
French protectorate of Cambodia is established.

Reign of King Chulalongkorn (Rama V) begins in 1868. The infrastructure, government, schools, and military are modernized. Employment of Western advisers to modernise Siam's administration and commerce. Railway network developed.
The Phra Pathommachedi is completed in Nakhon Pathom. Its height is 120 meters and it was the tallest stupa in the world until 1954.
King Chulalongkorn visits India.
Front Palace Crisis happens. Anglo-Siamese treaty over Chiang Mai is signed. Edict abolishing slavery is issued.
Prince Prisdang's memorial on a constitution prepared.
After 3 wars the British make Burma a province of British India on 1 January 1886. This ends the Burmese conflicts with Siam.
The Bangkok Times is founded in January 1887. It is the longest running English-language newspaper in Bangkok until World War II (30 Sep 1942).
Privy Purse Bureau established.
Ministerial council formed.

1893 Franco-Siamese crisis. French gunboats threaten Bangkok in the Paknam Incident. The French won which lead to substantial territorial concessions east of the Mekong river to the French which now forms most of Laos.
Interior Ministry founded.
The Paknam Railway is the first Siamese railway-line. It was constructed in 1891 and opened to the public by King Rama V on 11 April 1893.
King Chulalongkorn makes the first visit to Europe.
Holy Man's Rebellion. Armed rebellion of the Phu Mi Bun religious movement takes place.
Revolts break out in Phrae and the southern states revolt; Shangha Act passed.
The Franco-Siamese Treaty of 1904 officially demarcated clear boundaries between French Indochina and Thailand.
A series of reforms are implemented from 1874 until slavery is abolished by King Chulalongkorn in 1905.
Conscription edict issued for the Royal Thai Armed Forces.
Sun Yat-Sen visits Bangkok.
Anglo-Siamese treaty of 1909 finalizes Siam's border with British Malaya.
King Vajiravudh (Rama VI) accedes; Chinese strike in Bangkok.
Sra Pathum Airfield is the first airport in Thailand, established in 1911 at the site of the Sra Pathum Racecourse in Bangkok.
Plot uncovered in the military.
Thai Nationality Act passed; Surname Act passed.
Chulalongkorn University founded.
The design of the national flag called Trairanga (thong trai rong, tricolour flag) was adopted on 28 September 1917.
Siam becomes an ally of the United Kingdom in World War I.
Siamese contingent established to fight on the Allied side in Europe. The first 'political newspaper' is published.
Prince Damrong's history book Our Wars with the Burmese (Thai Rop Phama) is first published.
The Grand Palace in Bangkok is completed. The monarchy of Thailand was permanently settled there from 1782 until 1925. Many new buildings were added by various kings.
The first Siamese commercial airline was formed called the Aerial Transport of Siam Company (ATSC) on 3 July 1930.

The Siamese Revolution is a bloodless coup d’état against the absolute monarchy of King Prajadhipok. It ends centuries of absolute royal rule. A Constitutional monarchy is officially established and democracy with parliamentary government.
The Boworadet Rebellion, aimed at restoring an absolute monarchy, is put down by the ruling People's Party, a military-bureaucrat alliance.
The first two submarines of the Royal Siamese Navy (Matchanu-class) were completed and delivered on 4 September 1937. These were built by Mitsubishi Heavy Industries.
Siam officially changes its name to Thailand which means “Land of the Free”.
The Thai National Anthem in its current form was adopted on 10 December 1939.

Franco-Thai War begins in October 1940. After a sporadic battle between Thai and French forces, culminating in the Thai invasion of Laos and Cambodia in January 1941. Thailand successfully occupies the disputed territories in French Indochina.

Japan uses its influence with Vichy France to obtain concessions for Thailand in May 1941. Thailand annexes the territories Lan Chang Province, Nakhon Champassak Province, Phra Tabong Province, and Phibunsongkhram Province from Laos and Cambodia.

Japanese invasion of Thailand on 8 December 1941 during World War II. After negotiations Thailand lets Japanese advance towards the British-controlled Malay Peninsula, Singapore and Burma. Thailand deploys troops to fight on the Japanese side against Allied forces and became a member of the Axis Powers.
Thailand declares war on Britain and the United States, but the Thai ambassador in Washington refuses to deliver the declaration to the U.S. government.
Thailand annexes Saharat Thai Doem (Burma), and Sirat Malai (Malaysia), including Saiburi (Kedah State).
Thai envoy Wan Waithayakon attends the Greater East Asia Conference in Tokyo from 5 to 6 November 1943.
Thailand takes back the declaration of war against the United States and Britain. After the war, it becomes an ally of the U.S.
End of World War II. Thailand is compelled to return the territories it has seized from Laos, Cambodia, and Malaya. The exiled King Ananda Mahidol returns.

In 1946, Thailand agreed to cede the territories regained during Japanese presence in the country as the price for admission to the United Nations. Consequently, all wartime claims against Thailand were dropped and the country received a substantial package of U.S. aid.
King Ananda is assassinated in a mysterious shooting incident.
King Bhumibol Adulyadej becomes monarch aged 18. During his 70-year reign, Thailand has 10 coups and 17 constitutions.
The Bangkok Post, an English-language daily newspaper published in Bangkok, Thailand, was founded on 1 August 1946.

Military coup by the royalist-military forces led by the wartime, pro-Japanese leader Plaek Phibunsongkhram. The military retains power until 1973. The royalist-military forces end the People's Party's political role.
"Lèse-majesté" laws against insulting the king, dating back to the days of absolute monarchy, are carried over into a new Criminal Code.
The first South East Asian Peninsular Games is hosted in Bangkok, Thailand from 12 to 17 December 1959, with more than 527 athletes and officials from 6 countries.
The Association of Southeast Asia (ASA) is formed on 31 July 1961 and consisting of Thailand, the Philippines, and Malaya.
ASEAN is created on 8 August 1967. Thailand is a founding member with Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Singapore. This is the successor of ASA.
The 4th South East Asian Games is hosted in Bangkok, Thailand on 9–16 December 1967.
United States sends troops to Thailand during the Vietnam War. Thailand permits the United States to use bases there. Thai troops fight in South Vietnam.

1970s peasant revolts in Thailand. Prime Minister Thanom Kittikachorn ignores their pleas to reduce their debt and ensure fair rice prices. The farmer representatives form the Farmers Federation of Thailand (FFT). The Land Rent Control Act (LRCA) is finally enacted in December 1974.

The 1973 Thai popular uprising in Bangkok has pro-democracy protests. There are bloody clashes between the army and demonstrating students. It ends in a crackdown with 77 casualties, according to official estimates. On 14 October, King Bhumibol intervenes and announces the resignation of the military government. Free elections are held, but the resulting governments lack stability. Political and economic blunders bring down the resulting civilian government just three years later.
8th South East Asian Games is hosted in Bangkok on 9–16 December 1975.
The military takes over the government again.

Two military leaders who were ousted in 1973, return to Thailand. Protests follow and dozens of people are killed on 6 Oct 1973. Later that day is a military coup. The king appoints a new prime minister. The maximum penalty for insulting the monarchy is raised from 7 to 15 years.
A period of military-royalist government ensues with some roles for elected politicians.
New constitution is promulgated.
Thailand had the fastest developing economy in the world for about a decade from the late 1980s to the early 1990s. The development rate was 8% from 1985 till 1995.
13th South East Asian Games is hosted in Bangkok on 8–17 December 1985.
The 17th military coup since 1932. The civilian Anand Panyarachun is installed as prime minister.
During the elections in September 1992, Chuan Leekpai (leader of the Democrat Party) is chosen as prime minister.

The Black May demonstrations against another coup. The clash between military forces and civilian demonstrators causes 50 civilian casualties. King Bhumibol subsequently intervenes; a period of democracy follows. The military leaves the government to the civilian politicians.

In this period, from 1993 to 1997, the country saw unprecedented, exceptional economic growth. The financial boom kept growing with time. Thailand enjoyed fast economic development with sound increments in GDP.
The government collapses. Banharn Silpa-archa of the Thai Nation Party is elected prime minister.
Prolonged floods occur in Bangkok for 2 months in 1995. It causes over US$400 million in property damage and slows the economy.
18th South East Asian Games is hosted in Chiang Mai, Thailand on 9–17 December 1995.
The population of Thailand passes the 60 million people milestone.
Banharn government is accused of corruption and resigns. Chavalit Yongchaiyudh of the New Aspiration Party wins the elections.
The 1997 Asian financial crisis: The Thai Baht currency falls sharply against the dollar, leading to bankruptcies and unemployment. The IMF steps in. Chuan Leekpai becomes prime minister.
The HTMS Chakri Naruebet is the first aircraft carrier of Thailand. It was commissioned into the Royal Thai Navy on 27 March 1997.
Thailand's banking system and economy is in freefall as the Baht loses half of its value.

Tens of thousands of migrant workers are sent back to their countries of origin. Prime Minister Chuan Leekpai includes the opposition in his administration to push economic reforms through. Thailand follows the established guidelines given by the International Monetary Fund to resuscitate its economy.
The Rama III Bridge is completed. It crosses the Chao Phraya River in Bangkok. It is the longest bridge in Thailand with a length of 2,170 m (7,120 ft).

Senators are democratically elected for the Senate for the first time. The populist Thai Rak Thai Party founded by Thaksin Shinawatra, won the national polls for the House of Representatives. Billionaire businessman Thaksin Shinawatra is elected prime minister and forms a coalition government. Within a few years, Thailand is riven by rival demonstrations between Thaksin's Red Shirt supporters and Yellow Shirt opponents, who call Thaksin corrupt and disloyal to the monarchy. These will drag on for a decade.
Muslim nationalists step up terror operations in Yala, Pattani and Narathiwat provinces (South Thailand insurgency).

The 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami causes a massive earthquake and tsunami which strikes the west-coast of Southern Thailand and several other countries in Southeast Asia. There were over 8,000 casualties in Thailand and widespread devastation to the infrastructure and the economy.
In January–March 2004, martial law is imposed in largely-Muslim southern provinces after over 100 casualties in a wave of terrorist attacks which are blamed on ethnic-Malay separatists.
The Thaksin administration wins a second four-year term in the general elections.
The Suvarnabhumi Airport in the Bangkok Metropolitan Region officially opened in 2006.
Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra accuses several army officers of plotting to kill him after police find a car containing bomb-making materials near his house.

Thaksin is accused for tax evasion. There are months of mass Yellow Shirt protests in Bangkok. In September–October 2006, military leaders stage a bloodless coup which overthrows the Thaksin administration. Meanwhile, Shinawatra is at the UN General Assembly. Retired General Surayud Chulanont is appointed interim prime minister by the military while a new constitution was drafted.
Martial law is lifted in more than half of the country.
In August 2007, voters approve a new, military-drafted constitution in a referendum.
During the December elections, the Thaksin-endorsed People's Power Party wins the post-coup elections.
24th South East Asian Games is hosted in Nakhon Ratchasima, Thailand on 6–15 December 2007.
February 2008, return to civilian rule after the December elections. In a parliamentary vote on 28 January 2008, Samak Sundaravej of the People's Power Party (PPP) is sworn in as prime minister.
Thai troops shoot two Cambodian soldiers in a firefight on the disputed border, near the Preah Vihear temple.

In August 2008, Thaksin flees to Britain with his family after failing to appear in court to face corruption charges. Thaksin returns to Thailand with his wife, but skips bail before being tried on charges of corruption and debasement. Thaksin was sentenced to two years in jail in absentia.

Yellow Shirt protestors block the terminals of Bangkok's two international airports for 10 days, causing widespread disruption. They end their occupation after a court dissolves the ruling pro-Thaksin party. A new government led by another party is formed. Abhisit Vejjajiva becomes prime minister.

In March–May 2010, mass protest of tens of thousands of Thaksin supporters - in trademark red shirts - paralyze central Bangkok with a month-long protest calling for early elections and Prime Minister Abhisit's resignation. Anti-government Red Shirts protests in central Bangkok are quelled by the army in May after two months of violence. It culminates in a crackdown by troops who storm the protesters' barricades which causes 91 casualties.

In July 2011, the pro-Thaksin Pheu Thai Party wins a landslide victory in the elections. Yingluck Shinawatra (sister of Thaksin Shinawatra) becomes the first female prime minister of Thailand. More anti-Thaksin protests follow.

2011 Thailand floods are caused by the landfall of Tropical Storm Nock-ten. The impact lasts for 175 days between 25 July 2011 – 16 January 2012. There are 815 deaths and property damage in 65 of Thailand's 77 provinces. The estimated damage costs is 1.425 trillion baht (US$46.5 billion).
The government cuts the guaranteed price for rice, provoking an angry reaction from farmers and protests in Bangkok.
February 2013, the Government and separatists in Southern Thailand sign a first-ever peace talks deal.

May 2014, the Constitutional Court of Thailand orders Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra and several ministers out of office over alleged irregularities in appointment of security adviser. The Thai army with army chief Prayuth Chan-ocha seize power in a coup.
The King Power Mahanakhon is recognized as the tallest building in Thailand (314 m) by the CTBUH on 4 May 2016 .
August 2016, voters approve a new constitution giving the military continuing influence over the country's political life.
October 2016, King Bhumibol Adulyadej, the world's longest reigning monarch, dies at the age of 88 after 70 years on the throne.
In December 2016, Crown Prince Vajiralongkorn is proclaimed king.
April 2017, King Vajiralongkorn signs the new, military-drafted constitution that paves the way for a return to democracy.

The Tham Luang cave rescue in June and July 2018 had a team of international rescuers save a group of young soccer players and their coach who were trapped in a flooded cave in Northern Thailand. The dramatic rescue mission involved a complex network of divers, engineers, and volunteers, and captured global attention.
March 2019, the general election sees former general Prayut Chan-o-cha returned to power as prime minister. Opposition parties complain that the process was rigged, which Prayuth denies.
November 2019, suspected separatists kill at least 15 people in southern Thailand. This is one of the country's worst terror attacks in years.

Thailand has a wave of anti-government protests led by young activists calling for democratic reforms and an end to military influence in politics. The protests were met with a crackdown by the authorities, including arrests and charges of lèse-majesté which carries severe penalties in Thailand.

Court dissolves the opposition Future Forward Party. Its founder Thanathorn Juangroongruangkit denies wrongdoing in separate criminal charges over criticism of the military. This causes student-led protests.
COVID-19 pandemic in Thailand. Thailand was the first country to report a case outside China, on 13 January 2020. There were a total of 34,715 deaths.
The Sappaya-Sapasathan is completed on 1 May 2021. It is the world's largest parliamentary building with 424,000 m2 of floor space.
The leader of the Pheu Thai Party, Paetongtarn Shinawatra becomes the 31st prime minister of Thailand.
Same-sex marriage is legalized by the House of Representatives, effective 23 January 2025. Thailand is the first country in Southeast Asia and the 38th in the world to legalize it.
2025 Myanmar earthquake causes at least 36 deaths and 33 injuries in Bangkok. There are 14,430 reports of building damage to the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration.
Archaeological evidence of Homo sapiens in central Burma.
Archaeological evidence suggests that cultures existed in Burma as early as 11,000 BC.
Iron-working settlements south of present-day Mandalay.
Beikthano city fortified by Pyu people who had entered the Irrawaddy valley from north; beginning of Pyu city-states
Pyu city of Halin in existence
The Pyu convert to Buddhism (to 400)
Mon migrations to Lower Burma from Haribhunjaya and Dvaravati (present-day Thailand) (to 900)
The Pyu of Sri Ksetra Kingdom launch the Burmese calendar with the start date of 22 March 638.
Pyu city-states (like Hanlin) destroyed by Nanzhao raids
Pyinbya founds Pagan (Bagan)
Earliest evidence of Pagan walls
Earliest evidence of Burmese alphabet (according to an 18th-century recast stone inscription)
Pagan sends embassy to Song court at Bianjing
Earliest evidence of Burmese alphabet (at the Mahabodhi Temple, India)
Anawrahta ascends to Pagan throne
Anawrahta founds Pagan Kingdom including, Thaton, near Shan States, North Arakan, Malay Peninsula (to 1060)
Anawrahta converted to Theravada Buddhism by Shin Arahan
Pagan conquers Thaton Kingdom according to the Burmese chronicles
Anawrahta helps restart Theravada Buddhism in Ceylon
Rebellion in Lower Burma by Yamankan
Kyansittha becomes king
Kyansittha builds Ananda Temple
Earliest inscription of the word Mranma (Myanmar) in Mon script.
Burmese embassy to Song China
Myazedi inscription, earliest evidence of a more settled Burmese alphabet
Pagan restores Letyaminnan to north Arakanese throne
Thatbyinnyu Temple by Alaungsithu is complete.
Affirmation of Burman leadership of Pagan: Burmese becomes the primary written language, replacing Mon and Pyu
Narapatisithu founds the Royal Burmese Armed Forces, the first known standing army in Burmese history
Ceylonese raids to Bassein (Pathein)
Schism develops in Burmese Buddhism; majority of monks shift to Mahavihara school
The word Mranma first appears in Burmese
Dhamaavisala Dhammathat code of law compiled
Kyaukse weir built
Sithu II dies and Htilominlo succeeds
Htilominlo builds Htilominlo Temple, the last of the great temples
Kyaswa becomes king of Pagan
Narathihapate placed on Pagan throne
First mention of Mian (for Mranma) in Chinese
The first Mongol invasion begins
Thawun Gyi and Thawun Nge found Toungoo (Taungoo) as a frontier outpost
Second Mongol campaign begins
Wareru seizes governorship of Martaban (Mottama)
Pagan and Mongol commands sign ceasefire agreement
Burmese embassy led by Shin Ditha Pamauk leaves for Beijing
The Pagan Empire acknowledges suzerainty of the Mongol Empire
Wareru declares independence and founds Kingdom of Ramanya
King Narathihapate is assassinated
Kyawswa becomes king of Pagan
Wareru receives recognition as a vassal of Sukhothai
Wareru and Tarabya decisively defeat a major Pagan invasion
Kyawswa receives recognition by the Mongol Emperor as a Mongol vassal
Kyawswa overthrown and Myinsaing Kingdom founded
Ramanya receives recognition as a tributary of the Mongols
Saw Hnit placed as Myinsaing's puppet king of Pagan
Last Mongol invasion begins
Mongol forces retreat from Myinsaing
Mongols evacuate Tagaung, retreat to Yunnan
Wareru is assassinated and Hkun Law succeeds the Martaban throne
Athinkhaya dies
Saw O becomes king of Martaban
Thihathu founds Pinya Kingdom
Sagaing secession begins
Saw Yun's completes fortification of capital Sagaing
Saw Zein become king of Martaban
Tarabya I becomes king of Sagaing
Martaban defeats Sukhothai; throws off nominal allegiance to Sukhothai
Uzana I abdicates Pinya throne
Kyawswa I becomes undisputed ruler of Pinya
Kyawswa II becomes king of Pinya
Thihapate becomes king of Sagaing
Massive Shan raids into Upper Burma begin (to 1368)
Kyawswa II dies and Narathu succeeds Pinya throne
Binnya U raises the height of the Shwedagon Pagoda to 66 feet
Byattaba seizes Martaban; Binnya U sets up camp at Donwun
Maw forces sack Sagaing
Maw forces sack Pinya
Thado Minbya takes over Pinya
Thado Minbya founds Ava Kingdom
Swa Saw Ke becomes king of Ava
Byattaba drives Binnya U out to Pegu (Bago)
Shan state of Kale becomes tributary of Ava
North Arakan asks for a Burmese regent
Princess Maha Dewi becomes regent of Hanthawaddy Pegu
Razadarit becomes king of Pegu
Forty Years' War between Ava and Hanthawaddy Pegu begins
Razadarit consolidates all three Mon-speaking regions in Lower Burma
Tarabya becomes king of Ava
Minkhaung I becomes king of Ava
Arakan vassal to Ava or Hanthawaddy Pegu (To Ava: 1406–1407, 1412–1413; To Pegu 1407–1412; 1413–1422/(1430?) (to 1430)
Ava conquers Shan States of Mohnyin, Mogaung, Hsipaw
Minye Kyawswa killed in action
Min Saw Mon founds city of Mrauk-U
Mrauk-U conquers Thandwe, unifying the entire Arakan coast for the first time
Mrauk-U conquers Chittagong
Chinese invade Upper Burma, demanding surrender of a runaway Shan chief. His dead body was given up. Chinese records say events occurred in 1448–1449
Binnya Kyan increases the height of the Shwedagon Pagoda to 302 feet
Rise of early Burmese vernacular literature
Multiple rebellions by its vassals against Ava's rule. Prome, Yamethin and Mohnyin break away (to 1490)
Thado Minsaw successfully breaks away from Ava, founds Prome Kingdom
Mingyi Nyo becomes ruler of Toungoo; stays loyal to Ava
Narapati II becomes king of Ava
Ava cedes Kyaukse to Toungoo to buy its loyalty, and cedes Shwebo District to Mohnyin
Toungoo declares independence from Ava
Confederation of Shan States conquers Ava, and installs Thohanbwa as vassal king
Tabinshwehti becomes king of Toungoo
Toungoo–Hanthawaddy War (1534–41) begins
Toungoo forces capture Pegu; Toungoo–Ava War (1538–45) begins
Pegu made capital of Toungoo Kingdom
Toungoo forces capture Martaban
Toungoo forces invades Arakan
Min Bin and Tabinshwehti agree to a truce
First Burmese invasion of Siam begins
Burmese and Siamese commands agree to a truce
Tabinshwehti is assassinated
Bayinnaung takes Toungoo
Bayinnaung captures Ava, and annexes Upper Burma
Bayinnaung annexes cis-Salween Shan States; abolishes animal sacrifice at Popa Hill and human sacrifice at Shan Hills
Bayinnaung annexes Lan Na
Bayinnaung captures farther Shan States (Kengtung and Chinese Shan states)
The Ayutthaya Kingdom becomes Burmese vassal following the Burmese–Siamese War (1563–64)
Burmese forces capture Vientiane, capital of Lan Xang
Pegu learns of Siamese rebellion
Burmese–Siamese War (1568–69) restores Burmese rule in Siam
Burmese forces capture Vientiane
Bayinnaung dies, and his eldest son Nanda succeeds
Siam declares independence
Repeated Burmese invasions fail to reconquer Siam. Siam regains Tenasserim coast up to Mawlamyaing
All regions of the kingdom now in revolt

Fall of First Toungoo Empire after Pegu sacked by the Arakanese and Toungoo (city) forces. Siam captures the entire Tenasserim coast to Martaban. Arakanese capture delta ports; appoint Portuguese mercenary de Brito governor of Syriam
Siamese invasions take Martaban (1600) and Lan Na (1602) (to 1605)
Nyaungyan restores central rule to Upper Burma and Shan States (to 1606)
De Brito at Syriam declares independence from Arakan, repels Arakanese attacks (to 1605)
Portuguese mercenary Tibao captures Sandwip in East Bengal, northernmost Arakanese territory
Anaukpetlun captures Portuguese Syriam
Anaukpetlun recaptures the Tenasserim coast down to Tavoy, and all of Lan Na
Min Khamaung recovers Sandwip. Beginning of Arakanese raids on Dakha
English East India Company sends a representative to Pegu
Arakanese sack Dakha
English and Dutch East India companies open branches in Burma
Capital moved to Ava from Pegu
Thalun's revenue inquest
Arakanese use coined currency
Yongli Emperor of Ming China given refuge at Sagaing
Renegade Ming forces occupy near Shan states and attack Ava
Surrender of the Yongli Emperor to Qing forces
Siamese invasion of Lan Na and Tenasserim repelled (to 1664)
Mogul Empire defeats Arakan and captures Chittagong Province
English and Dutch East India companies close branches in Burma
Dutch East India Company closes its branch in Arakan
French East India Company opens a branch in Syriam
English open a branch in Syriam
Meiteis raid Upper Burma (to 1749)
Lan Na revolts; defeats Ava's attacks (1727–1728) and (1731–1732)
China annexes northern Shan States (present-day Kachin State, northern Shan State, and trans-Salween Shan State)
The Mon of Lower Burma break away, found Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom

Restored Hanthawaddy gradually pushes upcountry and captures Ava, ending the Tougnoo dynasty. The Siamese move up their control up the Tenasserim coast, taking Tavoy and then Martaban by 1751 (to March 1752)
Alaungpaya founds the Konbaung dynasty
Toungoo dynasty falls
Konbaung-Hanthawaddy War begins
English seize Negrais
Alaungpaya captures Dagon, having conquered the Irrawaddy delta in April
Alaungpaya captures French-defended Syriam.
Alaungpaya sends a punitive expedition to Manipur
Pegu captured; end of Restored Hanthawaddy
Konbaung armies overrun Manipur, reassert Burmese authority in northern Shan States which had been annexed by the Chinese in the 1730s (to 1759)
English driven out at Negrais
Burmese invasion of Siam falls short; regains the Tenasserim coast to Tavoy
Lanna rebellion put down
Burmese armies capture Laotian states of Luang Prabang and Vientiane
Hsinbyushin puts down a rebellion in Manipur
Capital moved to Ava
Start of Burmese–Siamese War (1765–67)
Start of Chinese invasions (1765–69) of Burma
Burmese armies sack Ayutthaya; end of Ayutthaya Kingdom
Burmese armies withdrawn from Siam and redeployed to the Chinese front. Burmese defenses against the Chinese invasions held. Siam recaptures all of its territories (except Tenasserim) (to 1770)
End of Sino-Burmese War
Rebellion in Manipur put down
Lan Na (Chiang Mai) revolts, seeks and receives Siamese help.
Hsinbyushin raises the Shwedagon Pagoda to its present height
Another Burmese invasion of Siam fails; Southern Lan Na becomes Siamese vassal (to 1776)
Laotian states (Luang Prabang and Vientiane) stop paying tribute, switch sides to Siam
Capital moved to Amarapura
Konbaung armies capture Mrauk U, ending five centuries of Arakanese independence
Bodawpaya's invasion of Siam fails; Lan Na now firmly in Siamese camp (to 1786)
Defeats Siamese invasion of Tenasserim
Resumes diplomatic relationship with China
Defeats another Siamese invasion of Tenasserim
Burmese invasion of Lan Na and Luang Prabang fails
Ceylonese monks seek ordination at Amarapura
Siamese invasion of Kengtung fails (to 1804)
Burmese invasion of Junkceylon (Phuket) fails (to 1812)
Burma annexes Manipur
Assam becomes tributary to Burma
Burmese put down rebellions in Assam and Manipur
Burmese put down another rebellion in Assam, and make it a Burmese province
Start of First Anglo-Burmese War
End of First Anglo-Burmese War; Burma cedes Arakan, Assam, Manipur and Tenasserim
Defeats Siamese invasion of Kengtung (to 1855)
Second Anglo-Burmese War; British seize Lower Burma
British expand Rangoon (modern-day downtown Yangon)
Mindon moves capital to newly founded city of Mandalay
Head of reform movement, Crown Prince Kanaung is assassinated.
Fifth Buddhist council convenes
Mindon cedes Karenni States to the British to avoid annexation
Rangoon College founded
Third Anglo-Burmese War; end of Burmese monarchy
British "pacification" of Burma (to 1896)
Burma is proclaimed a British colony. February: Burma is proclaimed a province of British India
First Rangoon University strike
The Dyarchy reforms begin
Nationalist and leftist Dobama Asiayone founded
Peasants' rebellion (to 1932)
Second Rangoon University strike
Burma is separated from British India and becomes a separate colony
Third Rangoon University strike and nationwide strikes
Burma Independence Army formed with Japanese help
Japanese occupation of Burma. Thai occupation of Kengtung (to 1945)
Return of British rule
Panglong Agreement signed by Shan, Kachin, Chin and Burman leaders to gain independence from the British
Aung San and most of his cabinet assassinated. U Nu and his AFPFL party prepare to take power from the British by finishing Burma's first constitution
1947 Constitution guarantees the Federated Shan States (later Shan and Kayah states), Kachin State, and Karen State, the right to secede after a period of ten years after independence
Burma gains independence from the United Kingdom with U Nu as Prime Minister
Insurgencies begin
Burmese Army repels Nationalist Chinese invasion of Shan State (to 1961)
Caretaker government, led by army Chief of Staff General Ne Win, formed following a split in the ruling AFPFL party. (Caretaker Gov. rule until 1960)
U Nu's party faction wins decisive victory in 1960 elections, but his promotion of Buddhism as the state religion and his tolerance of separatism angers the military.
U Thant becomes 3rd Secretary-General of the United Nations. Yangon hosts Second Southeast Asian Peninsular Games

Democratically elected government of U Nu is overthrown by Ne Win, who abolishes the federal system and inaugurates "the Burmese Way to Socialism" – nationalising the economy, forming a single-party state with the BSPP as the sole political party, and banning independent newspapers
Government guns down student protesters
Yangon hosts Fifth Southeast Asian Peninsular Games
Ne Win proclaims a new constitution. Chin Special Division becomes Chin State; Mon State is created out of Tenasserim Division. Government guns down student protesters following U Thant's death
Repeated demonetization of higher denomination kyat notes; Intensification of economic hardship on general populace (to 1987)
Nationwide uprising brings down Ne Win's government. Military crushes protests, forms a ruling junta, promises elections
Junta changes the English spellings of geographic names, including the country's name (to Myanmar)
National League for Democracy wins 82% of the seats in the general election. Junta refuses to hand over power, jails NLD leader Aung San Suu Kyi
Western nations and Japan begin economic sanctions against Myanmar
Aung San Suu Kyi is awarded the Nobel Peace Prize
Myanmar is admitted to ASEAN
A major bank run in private banking occurs
Bombings kill 11 people and injured 162
Junta moves the capital to Naypyidaw
Junta suppresses anti-government protests, killing scores of protesters, including Buddhist monks
2008 Constitution reserves 25% of the seats in a bicameral Hluttaw to the military.
Cyclone Nargis kills nearly 140,000 people and devastates the Irrawaddy delta
1st Kokang incident occurs
Bombings kill 10 people and injured 178
Government changes country's flag and its official name is adopted as "Republic of the Union of Myanmar"
The 2010 general election gives the victory to military-backed USDP
Aung San Suu Kyi is released from house arrest
The first session of Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (parliament) convenes
An earthquake occurs in Shan State
Thein Sein becomes President of Burma
Reforms in Burma begins
Economic sanctions imposed by the European Union and the United States are eased
Prominent political prisoners including Min Ko Naing are released
National League for Democracy wins in by-elections
Aung San Suu Kyi becomes a lawmaker
Rakhine State riots occurs
A train crash kills at least 27 people and injured 80
Government suppresses copper mine protests
Tensions between Buddhist and Muslim flare into violent clashes in various cities
Bombings kill 3 people and injured 10
27th Southeast Asian Games takes place
7th ASEAN Para Games takes place
A nationwide census takes place (Total population 51,486,253)
Ninth East Asia Summit takes place
2nd Kokang incident occurs
Government suppresses education law protests
Severe flooding occur
The 2015 general election gives the victory to NLD
A major landslide kills at least 116 people
The second session of Pyithu Hluttaw (lower house) convenes
The second session of Amyotha Hluttaw (upper house) convenes
The second session of Assembly of the Union (Union Parliament) convenes
The second session of State and Region Hluttaws (regional parliaments) convenes
Htin Kyaw becomes President of Myanmar
Aung San Suu Kyi becomes State Counsellor of Myanmar (de facto prime minister)
A 7.7-magnitude earthquake in central Myanmar. Over 140 people died and 730 were injured in Myanmar.
The prehistoric clay pottery Buni culture (near present-day Bekasi) flourished in coastal northern West Java.

"Dvipantara" or "Yawadvipa", a mystic Hindu kingdom is mentioned in India's earliest epic, the Ramayana; Sugriva, the chief of Rama's army dispatched his men to Yawadvipa in search of Sita then later used by the Indianized islander of Java Island and kingdom of Portugal to name the island during the age of discovery.
A footprint of a kingdom in Java island according to Chinese records.
The Kutai Martadipura phase in East Kalimantan produced the earliest known stone inscriptions in Indonesia.
Several stone inscriptions were created in West Java. Among others, the Tugu inscription announce decrees of Purnavarman, the king of Tarumanagara, one of the earliest Indianized kingdom in Java.
A Tang dynasty Chinese source written by I-tsing, mentioned about Holing (Kalingga) kingdom, located somewhere on the northern coast of Central Java.
I-tsing visited Srivijaya and Malayu in Sumatra and Kedah in Malay peninsula on his way to Nalanda, India.

Dapunta Hyang Sri Jayanasa performed Siddhayatra as the journey to expand his influence. The event is mentioned in several inscriptions such as Telaga Batu inscription, Talang Tuwo inscription, and Kedukan Bukit Inscription. The beginning of Srivijaya hegemony over the maritime region around Malacca Strait and Sunda Strait.
Srivijaya launch naval invasion against Java, mentioned in Kota Kapur Inscription. Probably contributed to the end of Tarumanagara kingdom.
I-tsing returned to Srivijaya on his way back from India to China. In his record he reported that the kingdom of Malayu was captured by Srivijaya.
The Sumatra-based Srivijaya naval kingdom flourishes.
Wet-field rice cultivation, small towns and kingdoms flourish. Trade links are established with China and India.

Sojomerto inscription possibly dated around late 7th century discovered in Batang Regency, Central Java, mentioned about Dapunta Selendra, possibly the ancestor of Shailendra dynasty. The inscription was written in old Malay suggested Srivijayan link to this family.

Sri Indravarman King of Srivijaya send a letter to the Caliph Umar bin Abdul Aziz of the Umayyad Caliphate in Damascus, signing early ancient Indonesian official contact with Islamic world in the Middle East.
The Sanjaya dynasty is founded around this time according to the Canggal inscription.
The Hindu Mataram kingdom flourishes.
The construction of Borobudur started.

Java launched series of naval raids on ports of Dai Viet, Champa and Cambodia; Sontay in Tonkin (767); Nha Trang (774); captured Indrapura in Cambodia (770); Phan Rang (787). The naval raids was probably launched by Shailendran-Srivijayan Maharaja Dharmasetu or Dharanindra.
Kalasan temple constructed according to Kalasan inscription.
The Manjusrigrha (Sewu) temple is completed according to Manjusrigrha inscription.
The agriculturally based Buddhist Shailendra dynasty rules Sumatra and Java.
Borobudur is completed during the reign of Samaratungga.
Prambanan is completed. According to Shivagrha inscription Rakai Pikatan — the husband of Pramodhawardhani — defeated Balaputra.

Balaputra the Maharaja of Suvarnadvipa and the ruler of Srivijaya, constructs the buddhist temple and monastery in Nalanda India, on the land given by King Devapaladeva of Pala in Benggala, according to the Nalanda inscription.
Sumbing volcano erupted, according to Rukam inscription.
King Balitung created Mantyasih inscription containing the list of Mataram kings, moved the capital from Mamratipura to Poh Pitu, and expanded Prambanan temple.
The Warmadewa dynasty rules Bali.
During the reign of King Wawa, the capital of Mataram in Mamratipura was devastated, probably by the massive eruption of Mount Merapi.

Mpu Sindok moved the seat of power of the Mataram kingdom from Mamratipura in Central Java to Tamwlang in East Java and established Isyana Dynasty. The shift was probably as a result of the eruption of Mount Merapi and/or invasion from Srivijaya.
Mpu Sindok moved the capital again from Tamwlang to Watugaluh, both near bank of Brantas River in modern Jombang in East Java.
Dynastic marriage between princess Mahendradatta of Javanese Isyanas and king Udayana of Balinese Warmadewas.
King Dharmawangsa of Mataram kingdom launches a naval invasion on Palembang in an unsuccessful attempt to conquer Srivijaya.
Airlangga, son of King Udayana and Queen Mahendradatta was born in Bali.
Dharmawangsa commissioned the translation of the Mahabharata into Old Javanese.
Srivijaya successfully repelling the Dharmawangsa's invasion, the invasion ultimately unsuccessful.
King Dharmawangsa's Mataram kingdom falls under invasion of King Wurawari from Lwaram (highly possible Srivijayan ally in Java).
Airlangga establishes the Kingdom of Kahuripan.

Rajendra Chola, the Chola king from Cholamandala in South India, conquered Pannai and Kadaram from Srivijaya and occupied it for some time. The Cholas continued a series of raids and conquests of parts Srivijayan empire in Sumatra and Malay Peninsula.
Sanghyang Tapak inscription in the Cicatih River bank in Cibadak, Sukabumi, West Java, mentioned about the establishment of sacred forest and Kingdom of Sunda.
Airlangga divided Kahuripan into two kingdoms Janggala and Kadiri and abdicated in favour of his successors.
King Jayawarsa of Kadiri ascends to the throne.

King Kamesvara of Kadiri ascends to the throne. Janggala ceases to exist and united under Kadiri domination, highly possible under royal marriage. During his reign Mpu Dharmaja writes Kakawin Smaradahana, a eulogy for the king and become the inspiration of Panji cycle, the tales that spreads across Southeast Asia.
King Jayabaya of Kadiri ascends to the throne.
Battle of Genter, Ken Arok defeated Kertajaya, the last king of Kediri, thus established Singhasari kingdom Ken Arok ended the reign of Isyana Dynasty and started his own Rajasa dynasty.
Baab Mashur Malamo established The Kingdom of Ternate in Maluku.
King Kertanegara of Singhasari launched Pamalayu expedition against Melayu Kingdom in Sumatra.
King Kertanegara launched Pabali expedition to Bali, which integrated Bali into the Singhasari territory.
Kertanegara insult the envoy of Kublai Khan that demand Java to pay the tribute to Yuan Dynasty.
Jayakatwang, duke of Kediri, rebelled and killed Kertanegara, ended the Singhasari kingdom.
Marco Polo, on his voyage from China to Persia visited Sumatra and reported that on the northern part of Sumatra there were six trading ports including Ferlec, Samudera and Lambri.
Mongol invasion of Java, Kublai Khan of Yuan dynasty China, sent punitive attack against Kertanegara of Singhasari. The Mongol forces were repelled.
The coronation of Nararya Sangramawijaya as the monarch of Majapahit kingdom, marked the foundation of Hindu Majapahit kingdom in eastern Java.
Footprint of Islam state is present in northern tip of Sumatra.
King Jayanegara succeeds Kertarajasa Jayawardhana as ruler of Majapahit.
an Italian Franciscan friar, Mattiussi visited Sumatra, Java, and Banjarmasin in Borneo. In his record he described Majapahit kingdom.
Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi succeeds Jayanegara as ruler of Majapahit.
Hayam Wuruk, son of Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi was born.
Mount Kelud in East Java erupted.
Gajah Mada declared his Palapa oath.
Adityawarman moved the capital of Dharmasraya and established the kingdom of Malayupura in Pagarruyung, West Sumatra.

Hayam Wuruk, styled Sri Rajasanagara succeeds Tribhuwana Wijayatunggadewi as ruler of Majapahit; his reign is considered the empire's 'Golden Age'. Under its military commander Gajah Mada, Majapahit stretches over much of modern-day Indonesia.
Kingdom of Negara Dipa was established in South Kalimantan by Empu Jatmika.

In the Battle of Bubat, the Sundanese royal family were massacred by the Majapahit army under the order of Gajah Mada. This event led to the death of Sundanese King Lingga Buana and the princess Dyah Pitaloka Citraresmi that committed suicide.
The Old Javanese text Nagarakertagama is written.
Majapahit sends a punitive expedition against rebelling Palembang in Sumatra. Palembang's prince, Parameswara, flees to Singapura, eventually became king of Singapura for several years.
Wikramawardhana succeeds Sri Rajasanagara as ruler of Majapahit.
Majapahit launched an invasion to Singapura. Parameswara (later Iskandar Syah) flees, eventually finding his way to Malacca and establishing it as a major international port.
Paregreg war, Majapahit civil war of succession between Wikramawardhana against Wirabhumi. (to 1406)
The first voyage of Zheng He, a massive Ming dynasty naval expedition visited Java, Palembang, Malacca, Aru, Samudera and Lambri. (to 1433)
Queen Suhita succeeds Wikramawardhana as ruler of Majapahit.
Wijayaparakramawardhana, succeeds Suhita as ruler of Majapahit.
Rajasawardhana, born Bhre Pamotan, styled Brawijaya II succeeds Wijayaparakramawardhana as ruler of Majapahit.
Reign of Rajasawardhana ends.
Girishawardhana, styled Brawijaya III, becomes ruler of Majapahit.
Singhawikramawardhana, succeeds Girishawardhana as ruler of Majapahit.
Reign of Singhawikramawardhana ends.
Islam becomes Indonesia's dominant religion.
Around late 15th century Bujangga Manik manuscript was composed, tell the story of Jaya Pakuan Bujangga Manik, a Sundanese Hindu hermit journeys throughout Java and Bali.

The Portuguese king sends Diogo Lopes de Sequeira to find Malacca, the eastern terminus of Asian trade. After initially receiving Sequeira, Sultan Mahmud Syah captures and/or kills several of his men and attempts an assault on the four Portuguese ships, which escape. The Javanese fleet is also destroyed in Malacca.
Afonso de Albuquerque after sailing from Portuguese Goa conquers the Sultanate of Malacca with a force of 1,200 and seventeen or eighteen ships.

The first Portuguese exploratory expedition was sent eastward from Malacca to search for the 'Spice Islands' (Maluku) led by Francisco Serrão. Serrao is shipwrecked but struggles on to Hitu (northern Ambon) and wins the favour of the local rulers.
The Portuguese established a trading post in the village of Lamakera on the eastern side of Solor as a transit harbour between Maluku and Malacca.
Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah of Aceh begins an expansionist campaign capturing Dayak on the west Sumatran coast, and the pepper and gold producing lands on the east coast.
The establishment of Banjar Sultanate in South Kalimantan with Sultan Suriansyah as the first king.
Ferdinand Magellan's expedition reaches Maluku and after trade with Ternate returns to Europe with a load of cloves.
The Portuguese ally themselves with the rulers of Ternate and begin construction of a fort.
Luso Sundanese Treaty signed between Portugal and Sunda Kingdom granted Portuguese permit to build fortress in Sunda Kelapa

The Portuguese in Ternate depose Sultan Tabariji (or Tabarija) and send him to Portuguese Goa where he converts to Christianity and bequeaths his Portuguese godfather Jordao de Freitas the island of Ambon.
Francis Xavier works among the peoples of Ambon, Ternate and Morotai (Moro) laying the foundations for a permanent mission. (to 1547)
